title: Project: sensor log tool
lesson:
In Level 1 you built a sensor report that kept running totals, because a tiny board can't store a whole log. Now you're on the PC side: the log arrives from a water tank, a greenhouse or a cold room at a clinic, it can be any length, and you want to keep every reading so you can look back. That needs everything from this level: a growing array, a linked list, out-parameters, and memory that ends up fully freed.

**The input.** The first number is the **alarm limit**. Every number after it is a reading, until the input ends:

```
30
18.5
22.0
31.0
25.0
26.5
34.0
```

**What the program keeps:**
- a `Readings` dynamic array (`vals`, `len`, `cap`) that grows with the safe realloc pattern, starting at 8 and doubling;
- an `AlarmList`: a linked list of every reading **above** the limit, in the order they arrived. It keeps a `tail` pointer as well as `head`, so adding at the end is instant instead of walking the whole list each time. Each alarm remembers which reading it was (counting from 1) and its value.

**The report:**

```
readings 6
min 18.5
max 34.0
average 26.2
alarms 2
alarm at reading 3: 31.0
alarm at reading 6: 34.0
live allocations 0
```

Numbers have one decimal place. With no readings at all (or not even a limit), print `no readings` instead of the six summary lines. The last line is always `live allocations` followed by Archie's counter, printed **after** you free everything. If it isn't 0, something leaked.

**How to build it.** Professionals build a tool like this in pieces and test each piece before joining them, so the project has three parts:
1. The readings array: add, stats (with out-parameters for min, max and average), free.
2. The alarm list: add at the tail, free the whole list.
3. The program: paste your pieces in, write `main`, and print the report.

**Ownership plan, written down first:** `main` owns the Readings and the AlarmList. `readings_free` frees the array; `alarms_free` frees every alarm node. Both reset their struct to empty. Nothing else allocates. With a plan like this, "where does this get freed?" always has a one-line answer.

Once it works, this is a real tool: point it at a log file with `sensorlog < tank.txt` and it tells you what happened overnight.

notes: The readings go into a growing heap array with the safe realloc pattern.
Capacity starts at 8 and doubles, exactly like the project.
Alarms count readings from 1 (i + 1), the way people number them.
The real tool keeps alarms in their own linked list instead of searching again.
Everything allocated is freed before main ends.

exercises.title: Part 1: the readings array
exercises.prompt: With Readings and readings_init given, write three functions. int readings_add(Readings *r, double v): append v, growing with my_realloc when full (capacity 8 at first, then double; safe pattern); return 1, or 0 if memory runs out. int readings_stats(const Readings *r, double *lo, double *hi, double *avg): if there are no readings return 0; otherwise store the smallest, largest and average and return 1. void readings_free(Readings *r): free with my_free and reset to empty.

tests.call: ({ Readings r; readings_init(&r); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) readings_add(&r, i * 1.5); int x = r.len * 100 + r.cap; readings_free(&r); x; })
tests.name: 20 readings, capacity 32

tests.call: ({ Readings r; readings_init(&r); double v[] = {18.5, 22.0, 31.0, 25.0, 26.5, 34.0}; for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) readings_add(&r, v[i]); double lo = 0, hi = 0, avg = 0; readings_stats(&r, &lo, &hi, &avg); readings_free(&r); lo * 10000 + hi * 10 + avg / 1000; })
tests.name: min, max, average

tests.call: ({ Readings r; readings_init(&r); double lo = -1, hi = -1, avg = -1; int ok = readings_stats(&r, &lo, &hi, &avg); ok * 100 + lo + hi + avg; })
tests.name: no readings: 0, outputs untouched

tests.call: ({ Readings r; readings_init(&r); readings_add(&r, -4.0); readings_add(&r, -9.5); double lo, hi, avg; readings_stats(&r, &lo, &hi, &avg); readings_free(&r); lo * 100 + hi; })
tests.name: all negative
tests.hint_if_fail: Start min and max from the first reading, not 0.

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; Readings r; readings_init(&r); for (int i = 0; i < 5000; i++) readings_add(&r, i); int during = live_allocs - before; readings_free(&r); during * 100 + (live_allocs - before) * 10 + (r.vals == NULL) + r.len + r.cap; })
tests.name: one block, freed and reset

hints: readings_add is unit 4's list_push with doubles and a starting capacity of 8.
readings_stats: if (r->len == 0) return 0; then *lo = *hi = r->vals[0]; and loop with a total.
readings_free: my_free(r->vals); then reset vals, len and cap.

exercises.title: Part 2: the alarm list
exercises.prompt: With Alarm, AlarmList and alarms_to_text given (start with AlarmList a = {NULL, NULL, 0};), write int alarm_add(AlarmList *a, int index, double value): a new Alarm (my_alloc) added at the END using the tail pointer (no walking), count goes up, return 1 (0 if memory runs out). Then void alarms_free(AlarmList *a): free every alarm and reset head, tail and count.

tests.call: ({ static char b[200]; AlarmList a = {NULL, NULL, 0}; alarm_add(&a, 3, 31.0); alarm_add(&a, 6, 34.0); alarms_to_text(&a, b); alarms_free(&a); b; })
tests.name: in arrival order

tests.call: ({ AlarmList a = {NULL, NULL, 0}; for (int i = 1; i <= 7; i++) alarm_add(&a, i, 40.0); int r = a.count * 100 + a.tail->index * 10 + (a.tail->next == NULL); alarms_free(&a); r; })
tests.name: count and tail
tests.hint_if_fail: After adding, a->tail must point at the new alarm.

tests.call: ({ static char b[200]; AlarmList a = {NULL, NULL, 0}; alarm_add(&a, 1, 50.5); alarms_to_text(&a, b); int same = a.head == a.tail; alarms_free(&a); same ? b : "head and tail differ"; })
tests.name: first alarm is head and tail

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; AlarmList a = {NULL, NULL, 0}; for (int i = 0; i < 30; i++) alarm_add(&a, i, 1.0); alarms_free(&a); (live_allocs - before) * 100 + a.count * 10 + (a.head == NULL && a.tail == NULL); })
tests.name: frees and resets

tests.call: ({ static char b[200]; AlarmList a = {NULL, NULL, 0}; alarm_add(&a, 2, 33.0); alarms_free(&a); alarm_add(&a, 9, 35.0); alarms_to_text(&a, b); alarms_free(&a); b; })
tests.name: usable again after freeing
tests.hint_if_fail: alarms_free must set head and tail back to NULL.

tests.call: ({ static char b[50]; AlarmList a = {NULL, NULL, 0}; alarms_free(&a); alarms_to_text(&a, b); b; })
tests.name: freeing an empty list

hints: Make the node with next = NULL. If a->tail is NULL the list was empty: a->head = n.
Otherwise a->tail->next = n. Either way a->tail = n; a->count++;
alarms_free: walk from head saving next before each my_free, then a->head = a->tail = NULL; a->count = 0;

exercises.title: Part 3: the sensor log tool
exercises.prompt: Write the whole program described in the lesson. Paste your functions from parts 1 and 2 over the stubs, then write main: read the limit, then every reading (keep them in Readings; every reading above the limit becomes an alarm numbered from 1); print the report exactly as in the lesson (or no readings); free everything; and finally print live allocations followed by live_allocs. Grow the readings with my_realloc.

tests.name: exactly the limit isn't an alarm
tests.hint_if_fail: Alarms are readings ABOVE the limit: use >.

tests.name: 2000 readings
tests.hint_if_fail: The readings array must grow; and free both structures before printing the counter.

tests.why: Grow the readings array with my_realloc.

hints: Start from the stubs: paste readings_add, readings_stats, readings_free, alarm_add and alarms_free from parts 1 and 2.
Loop: while (scanf("%lf", &x) == 1) { readings_add(&r, x); if (x > limit) alarm_add(&alarms, r.len, x); }
Print with readings_stats; walk alarms.head for the alarm lines; then readings_free, alarms_free, and print live_allocs last.

quiz.q: Why does the AlarmList keep a tail pointer?
choices: So adding at the end is instant instead of walking the whole list
quiz.why: With tail, push_back doesn't need a walk.

quiz.q: Why print live_allocs only after freeing everything?
choices: Then any number but 0 means something leaked
quiz.why: The counter is a leak check.

quiz.q: Why build and test the pieces before writing main?
choices: main must be written last in C
A bug is easier to find in a small tested piece than in the whole program

quiz.q: The readings array has 8 slots, all full, and a 9th reading arrives. What happens?
choices: realloc grows the array to 16 and the reading is stored
quiz.why: The dynamic array doubles when full.

quiz.q: Who frees the alarm nodes in this design?
choices: alarms_free, called by main which owns the list
quiz.why: Write down the ownership plan: main owns, the free functions clean up.

cards.a: tmp = realloc(vals, new_cap * sizeof *tmp); check NULL; then vals = tmp.

cards.q: Append to a list with head and tail?
cards.a: if tail is NULL, head = n; else tail->next = n; then tail = n.
main owns Readings and AlarmList; readings_free and alarms_free release them.

cards.q: How do you know nothing leaked?
cards.a: The allocation counter is back to 0 after freeing everything.

explain: Explain how your sensor log tool uses memory from start to finish: what gets allocated, when it grows, and where each block is freed.
